predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, no fertility clinic is routinely offering IVF using human egg cells derived from a patient’s somatic cells (e.g., skin cells) via in‑vitro gametogenesis (IVG) in clinical practice. Research groups have generated functional egg and sperm cells from somatic or pluripotent cells in mice and other animals, and human IVG has advanced in vitro (e.g., creating primordial germ cell–like cells and early gamete precursors), but **no approved, routine clinical IVF protocol** exists yet for producing fully functional human eggs from skin cells and using them in patients.

However, the *normalized* prediction is explicitly about what will be routine "by roughly the late 2020s". The current date is still only 2025, so the time window for the prediction (late 2020s ≈ 2027–2029) has *not* arrived. Because we cannot yet observe whether this will become routine by that future period, the correctness of the prediction cannot be determined at this time.

Therefore, the appropriate status is: it is **too early to tell** whether his forecast about late‑2020s routine clinic use will prove right or wrong.
predictions.grok_explanation: The prediction targets 'roughly the late 2020s' (e.g., 2027-2029) for *routine* use in fertility clinics. As of Dec 2025, proof-of-concept lab success exists: OHSU researchers (Sep 2025) created 82 functional human oocytes from skin cells (iPSCs), fertilizable via IVF to early embryos ([OHSU news](https://news.ohsu.edu/2025/09/30/ohsu-researchers-develop-functional-eggs-from-human-skin-cells), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2025/09/30/science/human-skin-cells-egg-infertility)). However, no blastocyst development in most cases, no live births, and no routine clinical offerings. Related advances like Gameto's iPSC-derived ovarian support cells (Fertilo) achieved a live birth (May 2025) but support maturation, not oocyte creation from somatic cells ([REPROCELL](https://www.reprocell.com/news/worlds-first-live-birth-using-reprocells-stemrna-clinical-seed-ipscs-for-oocyte-maturation-outside-of-the-body)). Japan approved stem cell embryo research (Aug 2025), but clinical routine use is absent ([STAT News](https://www.statnews.com/2025/08/13/japan-human-embryos-stem-cells-controversy-ethics/)). Too early to evaluate; technology advancing but not yet routine.

predictions.explanation:
As of **30 November 2025**, the time window specified by the prediction (“in the next couple of years” / “by the late 2020s”) has not yet elapsed, so it is too early to know whether IVF will in fact become *significantly* simpler, less invasive, and much more widely available than in early 2025.

Current scientific progress supports that we are still in an early, experimental phase:

- In 2025, scientists for the first time turned human skin cells into egg-like cells that could be fertilised, a key in‑vitro gametogenesis (IVG) milestone. However, the embryos showed many abnormalities, and researchers stress this is only proof‑of‑concept and **estimate that such lab‑generated eggs are at least a decade away from being widely available as a treatment**. ([tribune.com.pk](https://tribune.com.pk/story/2569949/human-skin-cells-turned-into-fertilisable-eggs?utm_source=openai))
- The UK fertility regulator similarly concluded in 2025 that lab‑grown eggs and sperm are on the *brink of viability* as a research technology, but clinical use is still expected to be up to a decade away, not something available broadly in the mid‑2020s. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2025/jan/26/lab-grown-eggs-sperm-viability-uk-fertility-watchdog?utm_source=openai))

Because (1) the forecast’s horizon extends into the **late 2020s**, and (2) we are only partway through that period, with the decisive technologies (like lab‑generated eggs) not yet clinically deployed, the correct judgment as of now is **inconclusive** rather than right or wrong.

Howard Lutnick, serving as Commerce Secretary in Trump’s second term, publicly said Trump’s goal was no federal tax for anyone making under $150,000, and media coverage described this as an aspirational tax plan, not an enacted policy. ([newsweek.com](https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-tariffs-trade-administration-live-updates-2044066?utm_source=openai))

However, the major tax legislation actually passed under the new Trump administration so far is the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025. That law extends and tweaks the existing individual income tax system (originally set by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), adds targeted deductions (e.g., for tips, overtime, some car-loan interest, and certain seniors), but it does not set the federal income tax rate to 0 percent for people earning $150,000 or less. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act?utm_source=openai))

The IRS rate schedules for the 2025 tax year still show positive marginal income-tax rates starting at 10 percent, with higher brackets above that, and the IRS’s released brackets for 2026 likewise remain a normal progressive system; there is no blanket 0 percent federal income tax rate for all taxpayers at or below $150,000 in any filing status. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_schedule_%28federal_income_tax%29?utm_source=openai))

Because, as of November 30, 2025, no law or regulation has been implemented that actually reduces federal income tax to 0 percent for all U.S. taxpayers earning $150,000 per year or less, the prediction that such a Trump tax plan would be implemented as described is wrong.

predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, the large nationwide housing crash Chamath described has *not* occurred, but his time horizon (“the next phase of the cycle”) is vague enough that it could still play out in coming years.

Key facts:
- U.S. homeowners currently sit on roughly **$34–36 trillion in home equity**, an all‑time or near‑all‑time high, according to Federal Reserve–based estimates and industry analyses. One summary notes home equity at over **$35 trillion as of March 2025**, another puts it at about **$34.5 trillion in 2025**, and a Mortgage Bankers Association forecast says homeowners have accumulated about **$36 trillion** in equity. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_equity?utm_source=openai))
- For homeowners with mortgages (a subset of all homeowners), total net equity in Q2 2025 was about **$17.5 trillion**, with equity *down only 0.8% year‑over‑year*—a reduction of about **$141.5 billion**, not “trillions.” ([themortgagepoint.com](https://themortgagepoint.com/2025/09/15/uptick-in-u-s-housing-prices-drives-stalling-home-equity-growth/?utm_source=openai))
- National home‑price indexes show **slowing growth and some real (inflation‑adjusted) erosion**, but not a major nominal crash. The S&P CoreLogic Case‑Shiller National Index reported a **3.4% year‑over‑year gain in March 2025**, and later data show prices still up about **1.3–1.5% year‑over‑year** by late summer/early fall 2025, even though that growth now lags inflation. ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/index-announcements/article/sp-corelogic-case-shiller-index-records-34-annual-gain-in-march-2025/?utm_source=openai))
- FHFA’s own house‑price data for Q3 2025 show about a **3.3% year‑over‑year price increase**, which is why it raised conforming loan limits for 2026—again indicating slower appreciation, not a collapse in values. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/40875c1a64eec21dbbd351fd76e0ecf9?utm_source=openai))
- Equity markets did experience a sharp but brief selloff in early April 2025 tied to broad tariff hikes, temporarily erasing more than $3 trillion in stock‑market value, but major indexes recovered by mid‑May. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market_crash?utm_source=openai)) That episode has *so far* not been followed by a housing crash of the magnitude Chamath described.

Putting this together, U.S. housing is clearly cooling: price growth has nearly stalled in nominal terms, some metros have begun to see outright declines, and mortgage‑borrower equity ticked down slightly. But nationwide housing wealth is still near record highs, and the observed pullback has erased **hundreds of billions**, not **trillions**, of dollars of housing wealth. That means Chamath’s specific scenario (a “major downward correction” that “whacks” the housing market and wipes out *trillions* in wealth) **has not yet happened**.

However, because he did not give a specific deadline and framed it as the “next phase of the cycle,” it remains possible that a deeper correction could occur beyond November 2025. Since the absence of such a crash by this date does not conclusively falsify a cycle‑phase prediction with an open time horizon, the fairest classification today is **inconclusive (too early)** rather than definitively “wrong.”

- The FHFA House Price Index shows U.S. house prices **up 2.2% year‑over‑year in Q3 2025**, with a 0.2% quarterly increase, not a large decline. ([fhfa.gov](https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/u.s.-house-prices-rise-2.2-percent-year-over-year-up-0.2-percent-quarter-over-quarter?utm_source=openai))

- The S&P CoreLogic Case‑Shiller National Index shows home prices **still rising slightly (around 1.3–1.5% year‑over‑year) as of August–September 2025**, indicating cooling or flattening, not a crash. - FHFA’s increase in conforming loan limits for 2026 is based on a **3.3% rise in home prices from Q3 2024 to Q3 2025**, again inconsistent with a major nationwide drawdown. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/40875c1a64eec21dbbd351fd76e0ecf9?utm_source=openai))

In the episode transcript, Chamath talks about home prices being “whacked 30 or 40%” in the context of a broader future housing correction and policy changes, but **he does not specify a clear time horizon** for when that 30–40% national decline would occur. ([speakai.co](https://speakai.co/podcast-transcription/all-in-podcast/fixing-the-american-dream-with-andrew-schulz/?utm_source=openai))  

Because (1) as of November 30, 2025 there has been **no such 30–40% nationwide drop**, but (2) the prediction has **no explicit deadline** and housing cycles can take years, it is too early to definitively label the prediction as right or wrong. It has clearly **not come true yet**, but it **could still be falsified or fulfilled in the longer term**, so the fairest assessment at this time is **“inconclusive (too early).”**

predictions.explanation:
It’s too early to know whether this prediction is correct or not.

The claim is that, under current law and contribution/benefit patterns, the U.S. Social Security Trust Fund will become insolvent around **2032** ("going to go bankrupt in 2032"). Insolvency here means the trust fund reserves are depleted and the system can no longer pay **full** scheduled benefits, not that payments stop entirely.

As of **November 30, 2025**, that future date has not yet arrived, so the trust fund has not become insolvent and no definitive judgment about 2032 can be made.

For context, recent official projections are in the same general time frame but do **not** exactly match 2032:

- The **2024 Social Security Trustees Report** projects that the combined OASDI trust funds will be depleted in the mid‑2030s under current law (with the exact year depending on the report’s assumptions and whether you look at OASI alone or combined OASDI). After depletion, incoming payroll taxes would still cover roughly three‑quarters of scheduled benefits, but not 100%.
- Other analyses (e.g., from the Congressional Budget Office) have at various times projected depletion dates around the early‑to‑mid 2030s as well.

Because (1) the predicted year **2032** is still in the future and (2) projected depletion dates can shift with each new report and policy/economic change, this prediction cannot yet be judged as right or wrong.

The prediction said that during Trump’s 2025–2029 term, Elon Musk would *avoid open conflict with Trump* and would *not significantly break with or oppose Trump on any major public issue*.

In reality, by May–June 2025 Musk had publicly broken with Trump over the president’s flagship “Big Beautiful Bill” spending package. In a CBS interview and other comments, Musk called it a “massive spending bill” that increases the deficit and *undermines the work that the DOGE team is doing*, and he criticized it repeatedly on X.([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2025/05/28/trump-big-beautiful-bill-elon-musk-disappointing-doge/?utm_source=openai))  He also attacked the bill’s supporters in Congress, warning on X that members who campaigned on cutting spending but backed the bill would “lose their primary” and labeling them “LIAR[s]” in planned ads, which reporters noted as a direct challenge to Trump’s central legislative agenda.([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/2025/07/02/trump-musk-feud-musk-says-trumps-comments-about-him-are-just-plain-wrong/?utm_source=openai))

Soon after, Musk left the Trump administration; multiple outlets explicitly linked his exit and a broader Musk–Trump "fracture" to this clash over the bill.([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2025/05/28/elon-musk-exits-trump-administration-after-clash-over-big-beautiful-bill/?utm_source=openai))  Coverage of DOGE’s later shutdown likewise described it as following Musk’s falling‑out with Trump over the legislation.([time.com](https://time.com/7336327/doge-disbanded-elon-musk/?utm_source=openai))  Forbes further characterized the situation as a feud, quoting Musk saying Trump’s comments about him were “just plain wrong” and “disappointing.”([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/2025/07/02/trump-musk-feud-musk-says-trumps-comments-about-him-are-just-plain-wrong/?utm_source=openai))

Because Musk has already engaged in very public, high‑stakes opposition to Trump’s signature spending bill, openly criticized Trump’s stance, and exited the administration in a context described as a split or feud, he has *not* consistently maintained a cooperative, pro‑Trump posture or avoided major public breaks. A single clear counterexample is enough to falsify the prediction, even though the presidential term is not yet over.

predictions.explanation:
**Summary of the prediction**

Schulz’s claim is essentially conditional and long‑run:
- *When* the S&P 500 jumps ~15% in a short period and people see big portfolio gains,
- *then* U.S. public attention to transgender "bathroom" controversies will quickly and materially decline, becoming far less salient than economic gains.

**Did the market condition occur?**

Yes, at least once in the period since the episode’s March 15, 2025 release:

- After a sharp drawdown that left the S&P 500 about 19% below its February record on April 8, 2025, the index **rallied 19.6% over the next 27 trading days (to May 16)**, one of the biggest such short‑term gains in its history.
  ([nasdaq.com](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/stock-market-signal-says-sp-500-could-surge-higher-2025?utm_source=openai))
- By June 27, 2025, Reuters reported the S&P 500 at a **record high of 6,178.80**, more than **23.5% above its April 8 low**. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/sp-500-nasdaq-hit-record-highs-renewed-ai-bets-rate-cut-hope-2025-06-27/?utm_source=openai))  That clearly satisfies the “up ~15% in a short timeframe” condition and implies large paper gains for many retail portfolios.
- A later Reuters piece notes the S&P 500 was up about **12.3% for 2025** as of late November, reinforcing that 2025 featured strong equity performance overall. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/deutsche-bank-sees-sp-500-rising-8000-by-end-2026-2025-11-24/?utm_source=openai))

So the economic/market side of the prediction *has* been met, at least once.

**What happened with “bathroom” controversies in that environment?**

From early 2025 through late 2025 – including during and after the April–June rally – bathroom‑focused transgender controversies *remained active and visible*:

- **Ohio**: A bathroom‑restriction law (SB 104, "Protect All Students Act") that had been signed in November 2024 took effect on **February 25, 2025**, and generated new implementation coverage as schools changed policies. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Senate_Bill_104?utm_source=openai))
- **Wyoming**: HB 72 ("Protecting Privacy in Public Spaces Act") was signed **March 3, 2025** and took effect July 1, 2025, banning transgender people from using certain bathrooms aligned with their gender identity in public facilities, with continuing local media and activist attention. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming_House_Bill_72?utm_source=openai))
- **South Dakota**: On **March 21, 2025**, the governor signed HB 1259, restricting transgender people’s access to restrooms and changing rooms in public schools and state buildings, drawing national wire coverage and civil‑liberties criticism. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/823b8672ec78ebaca451c97704ff1a68?utm_source=openai))
- **Montana**: Early 2025 saw House Bill 121 – a new anti‑trans bathroom bill – advance in the legislature, framed in national reporting as part of a renewed wave of bathroom legislation. ([them.us](https://www.them.us/story/montana-first-state-advance-anti-trans-bathroom-legislation-2025?utm_source=openai))
- **Texas (the clearest test)**:
  - Texas Senate Bill 8 ("Texas Women’s Privacy Act") – a sweeping bathroom bill with **very large civil fines** – moved through a special session in August 2025 and passed the legislature on September 3. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_Senate_Bill_8_%282025%29?utm_source=openai))
  - Gov. Greg Abbott then **signed SB 8 into law on September 22, 2025**, making it – by several accounts – the most punitive bathroom law in the U.S., and prompting extensive state and national coverage, protests, and civil‑rights backlash. ([teenvogue.com](https://www.teenvogue.com/story/texas-gov-abbott-signs-trans-bathroom-bill-into-law?utm_source=openai))
- A contemporaneous overview notes that, as of July 1, 2025, **19 U.S. states** had transgender bathroom restrictions in force, underscoring that such policies remain a widespread and ongoing flashpoint rather than a forgotten issue. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathroom_bill?utm_source=openai))

In other words, even *after* the S&P’s strong rebound and into a period of record highs, bathroom bills were not only present but in some states at their **most intense and high‑profile** stage (especially Texas).

**What about relative public priorities?**

Poll data in 2025 do show the **economy and cost of living dominate voters’ stated priorities**, while LGBTQ issues, including trans/bathroom debates, rarely register as “top problems”:

- An October 2025 Reuters/Ipsos poll found **cost‑of‑living concerns (healthcare, housing, food, energy)** were named as the top political issue by about 40% of Americans, ahead of democracy, immigration, and crime. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/cost-of-living-worries-haunt-americans-ahead-midterms-reutersipsos-poll-finds-2025-10-24/?utm_source=openai))
- A June 2025 California survey, citing a national Reuters/Ipsos benchmark, similarly shows **political extremism/democracy, the economy/jobs, and immigration** as the leading “most important problems,” not bathroom or transgender issues. ([ppic.org](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/?utm_source=openai))
- Another large poll reported that many voters see Democrats as overly focused on matters like undocumented immigrants and LGBTQ+ rights rather than bread‑and‑butter concerns (border security, crime, economic costs, healthcare). ([nypost.com](https://nypost.com/2025/10/28/us-news/70-of-voters-think-the-democratic-party-is-out-of-touch-poll/?utm_source=openai))
- Broader work on the 2020s anti‑LGBTQ movement shows trans issues (including sports and youth medical care) are widely salient and polarized, but does not indicate they have vanished or sharply fallen from public debate in 2025. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020s_anti-LGBTQ_movement_in_the_United_States?utm_source=openai))

Crucially, **economic issues already dominated public concern before** the 2025 rally; there isn’t clear evidence of a *new* or *discrete* drop in attention to bathroom controversies specifically *because* of the market surge.

**Why the verdict is “ambiguous” rather than clearly right or wrong**

To label the prediction definitively right or wrong, we would need something like:

- Quantitative, time‑series measures of public or media attention specifically to *bathroom* controversies (e.g., issue‑salience polling categories or systematic coverage counts) **before and after** the S&P rally, and/or
- Evidence that these controversies either disappeared from legislation and media, or conversely became *more* central, in *direct correlation* with the S&P’s rally.

What we *do* know:

1. **The S&P condition clearly occurred.** There was at least one episode (April–June 2025) where the index surged well over 15% in a short window and hit record highs. ([nasdaq.com](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/stock-market-signal-says-sp-500-could-surge-higher-2025?utm_source=openai))
2. **Bathroom controversies demonstrably did *not* disappear.** Multiple states, especially Texas, advanced or enacted high‑profile bathroom bills with substantial media attention during and after that strong market period. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming_House_Bill_72?utm_source=openai))
3. **Economic issues remain the top stated concern**, but they already held that position; we lack strong evidence that bathroom issues became *materially less salient than before* in response to portfolio gains, as opposed to simply continuing as a parallel culture‑war track.

The problem is that Schulz’s claim is both:
- **Vague in timing and magnitude** ("how quickly," what counts as "materially" less salient, and compared to what baseline?), and
- **Open‑ended** ("in future periods" in general, not specifically *this* 2025 rally).

Given those ambiguities and the lack of precise salience data, we can’t conclusively say the prediction has been *empirically falsified*—but we also can’t say it has clearly come true. The best we can say is:

- The available evidence **does not show** that bathroom controversies were forgotten or clearly downgraded when the S&P 500 jumped.
- At least in 2025’s major rally, **both** strong market performance and intense bathroom‑policy fights co‑existed.

Because the conditional prediction is broad, loosely specified, and only partially testable with the data we have, the fairest classification at this point is **“ambiguous.”**

Available biographical and entertainment coverage of Andrew Schulz through late 2025 consistently notes that he and his wife Emma have **one child**, daughter Shiloh Jean, born in February 2024, with no mention anywhere of additional children.

Examples:
- Recent profiles and interviews describe Schulz as a father to a *baby girl* or *daughter* (singular), conceived via IVF, with no reference to more kids.  
- Multiple biographical pieces and features on Emma Turner likewise state that the couple "welcomed their first child" Shiloh in February 2024 and do not report any second or third child as of 2025.  
- A current encyclopedia-style entry lists one daughter, Shiloh Jean, born February 2024, and does not list any other children.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Schulz?utm_source=openai))

The prediction, however, is that Schulz **will** go on to have a second and third child at some point in the future. That is an open‑ended, forward‑looking claim. As of November 30, 2025, it has **not** come true (he still has only one publicly known child), but it also has **not** been falsified, because more children could still be born later.

Because the claim is about an event that could still occur in the future and there is no way yet to know whether it ultimately will or won’t happen, the correct status is **“inconclusive (too early)” rather than “right” or “wrong.”
